The analysis also revealed that certain types of light emission, such as the 3.4-micrometer signal, tend to be stronger in certain halo types and that the amount of light being scattered can vary depending on the size of the halo. In educational settings, traditional lectures incorporating live demonstrations offer an effective learning method by enabling students to engage with the material in a more dynamic and interactive way. However, the automatic analysis of these demonstrations presents a challenging task due to the diverse and dynamic nature of video and live writing data. To address this challenge, we have developed a large dataset comprising 100 multimodal lectures containing 1,200 live writing frames and 20,000 video frames, along with corresponding transcription scripts. This dataset aims to facilitate automatic analysis and empower educators to track student participation during presentations, monitor student learning, and provide real-time feedback. To achieve this goal, we have created two tracking modules: one for live writing and another for video analysis. A range of experiments were conducted, including object detection, recognition, and tracking, as well as NLP-based data association, to evaluate the performance of these modules. The results show that our proposed approach is capable of providing valuable insights in an educational setting, and the dataset and code are available for public access. The code can be found at https://github.com/ramin.tan/Multimodal_Lecture_Demonstrations_Dataset. ServiceX utilizes a modular design, with a database normalization system and a set of transformation modules tailored to specific question formats. This paper presents the underlying design of ServiceX and illustrates its practical applications, as well as discussing potential limitations. In addition, we provide an overview of the system's current implementation and future development roadmap. In contrast to other existing systems, ServiceX offers a more streamlined and automated process for generating exam questions. Our analysis indicates that ServiceX outperforms its competitors in terms of its speed, efficiency, and user-friendly interface. Furthermore, ServiceX has been successfully implemented in a real-world context, with a large-scale exam administered annually to over 100,000 students. In this paper, we also review the existing literature on this topic and highlight areas for further investigation. In summary, this paper presents a novel approach to exam question generation, with a focus on its design and implementation, and its potential for future research and development. The Earth's climate is constantly evolving due to ongoing changes, and monitoring its various parameters through satellite imagery helps scientists understand its dynamics better. AI algorithms are particularly useful in this process, as they can quickly analyze vast amounts of satellite data to identify trends and indicators of these shifts. To facilitate this research further, EarthNets is developing an open platform that utilizes cloud-native, containerized deep learning to provide an efficient and scalable means of modeling satellite imagery. This platform aims to offer a flexible and adaptable framework for scientists to analyze satellite data and gain insights into the planet's evolving conditions. EarthNets' architecture is designed to be robust and can handle a large volume of satellite image data, which it achieves by decoupling the system into three primary components: (1) data storage and (2) computation and (3) visualization tools that can be scaled up or down according to user needs. Furthermore, the platform allows users to access satellite data and associated models through a user-friendly interface, which includes a dashboard that displays the results of AI models and provides an easy-to-understand visual representation of findings. By offering an accessible deep learning platform for analyzing satellite data, EarthNets is poised to empower scientists to better monitor the planet's changing conditions. The goal of offline reinforcement learning is to develop an agent that performs optimally in a pre-defined static environment with fixed dynamics. This contrasts with online RL, where the environment's dynamics can change over time. This static environment setting is particularly useful when dealing with situations like robotic manipulation, where the agent cannot interact with the environment to adapt to changing conditions. This paper focuses on the minimax offline RL problem, which involves designing an optimal agent for a pre-defined environment to minimize its worst-case performance. This is distinct from the regret-based offline RL problem, which aims to develop an optimal agent for a set of pre-defined environments to minimize its average regret. The key difference between these problems lies in the potential for the dynamics to change across different environments in the regret setting, which is not a concern in the minimax setting since the agent operates within a single environment. This paper presents a first-order algorithm for the minimax offline RL problem, which leverages a policy gradient method to develop an optimal agent for the pre-defined static environment. This algorithm is shown to achieve a polynomial-time convergence rate of O(1/√T) and is computationally efficient, with a time complexity of O(BN^3d). This algorithm is particularly useful for solving problems with limited sample sizes, which is demonstrated through its application to robotic manipulation tasks. Additionally, this work establishes a completeness result for the offline RL problem, which is further discussed in the appendix. Overall, this research provides a comprehensive understanding of the offline RL problem, particularly when dealing with limited sample sizes. A novel circuit closure approach is presented that leverages bi-directional navigation between a starting and ending point. Initially, the agent's position is set and then they follow a predetermined route in reverse, back to the initial point. This method is paired with Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VSLAM) to enable the agent to gather visual data, perform loop closure detection, and refine its location estimation while navigating along the circuit path. To enhance the agent's circuit closure capabilities, a risk-aware path planning algorithm is employed, ensuring a safe and efficient route is taken. Extensive testing of this approach was conducted using a mobile robot in both indoor and outdoor environments, resulting in successful loop closure outcomes across all testing scenarios. Specifically, the results showed that the approach successfully detected loop closures at a rate of 100% for all tested paths. Furthermore, the approach was successful in detecting a 1.4 km long circuit in a real-world environment using a mobile robot equipped with an RGB-D camera. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first time a bi-directional circuit closure has been successfully implemented using a real-world robot. because the camera's sensor is overwhelmed by the incoming light, which results in 
noisy and distorted images. To address this issue, researchers have developed a new 
dataset consisting of paired low-light and well-lit images. The goal of this dataset 
is to enable the evaluation of methods that can accurately measure and reduce light 
intensity to produce images that are visually indistinguishable from those taken in 
well-lit conditions. To achieve this, a system was designed to simultaneously capture 
and illuminate pairs of low-light and well-lit images. The system uses a high-speed 
camera and flash unit, which rapidly adjusts the flash's aperture to minimize 
exposure disparities between the paired images. The resulting dataset is used to 
evaluate the effectiveness of various image processing methods, including noise 
reduction, tone mapping, and local contrast adjustment. The results demonstrate that 
these methods can significantly improve image quality, but also reveal limitations 
in their ability to accurately replicate the appearance of well-lit images. The 
dataset and accompanying code are publicly available at https://github.com/tonytang1543/

editing techniques. For a related project, please visit http://tinyurl.com/LLImageEditing.

This research paper introduces BilairTelOp, a bilateral teleoperation system that enables users to control and interact with a three-dimensional aerial robot in real-time. The system allows for the manipulation of an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) in any direction, providing the operator with precise control and haptic feedback. We address the complexities of controlling a three-dimensional autonomous aircraft in any orientation, regardless of its position. To achieve this, we developed a BilairTelOp client that translates the three-dimensional movement into two-dimensional commands, allowing the UAV to move freely in any direction. We also designed a BilairTelOp server that calculates and transmits the environment forces acting on the UAV to the client in real-time. By integrating a bilateral filtering algorithm, we ensured that the UAV receives timely and accurate feedback. We tested BilairTelOp in a series of experiments, where participants successfully performed aerial tasks and demonstrated the effectiveness of the system. Overall, BilairTelOp's ability to provide users with fine motor control, enhanced visual feedback, and real-time haptic feedback enables more accurate and precise interactions with three-dimensional aerial robots. Pretrained models like CLIP excel in image-text matching, yet struggle with adapting to new domains.  To address this limitation, research has focused on fine-tuning CLIP in specific areas, but this often requires substantial resources.  In contrast, our Domain Prompt Learning (DPL) approach enhances CLIP performance in new domains without needing to retrain.  DPL involves creating a simple prompt based on the target domain's keywords, which boosts accuracy on both seen and unseen areas.  DPL outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, achieving significant gains in accuracy on several benchmarks, particularly in open-set scenarios.  DPL's effectiveness stems from its ability to capture the underlying meaning of domain keywords and improve the model's understanding of unseen data.  DPL's simplicity and effectiveness make it a compelling alternative to existing domain adaptation methods, especially when resources are limited. The effectiveness of image dehazing methods is typically evaluated using two metrics, the EPIC and EPIC-Gloss, which measure the intensity of light and gloss separately. However, these measures are not entirely accurate due to their inability to accurately capture the full range of image dehazing quality. As a result, we have developed a new evaluation method that integrates these measures into a single, more comprehensive metric, eliminating the need for separate lightness and gloss assessments. Our approach involves creating a new divergence metric, the F1 partial divergence, which enables the use of only partially aligned reference images, overcoming the limitations of conventional full-reference quality metrics in the dehazing domain. The proposed metric, the F1 partial dehazing index, is then derived from this divergence metric, providing a single, comprehensive dehazing quality assessment. Through our experimental results, we have demonstrated that this new approach outperforms existing dehazing quality metrics, achieving more accurate and reliable results. The proposed method also has the advantage of requiring no human ratings, thereby facilitating the use of blind dehazing quality assessment. The breakthrough in dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) at room temperature has greatly expanded the capabilities of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) experiments. Despite this progress, several key limitations still exist. Notably, the range of solvable compounds is restricted due to the requirement for specific relaxation times and signal-to-noise ratios, while the use of certain hyperpennings is hampered by safety concerns. In this research, we have successfully developed an alternative DNP method that utilizes the P1 center in diamond as a hyperpennning source, allowing for the bulk-sensitive 13C NMR of large samples at room temperature. Notably, this technique has broad applicability, as it can be applied to extensive molecular structures and is not limited by relaxation times or signal-to-noise ratios, making it particularly suitable for the study of complex biological macromolecules. Additionally, the use of diamond hyperpennings eliminates the need for volatile chemicals and offers improved safety profiles. The technique has already been successfully applied to the bulk 13C NMR of a 1.5 gram sample of a protein, demonstrating its vast potential. We anticipate that this advancement will greatly expand the scope of DNP applications. This research introduces a control method for quadrupedal robots to enable smooth and efficient movement over various terrain. The proposed system consists of two layers: a high-level adaptive controller and a low-level motion tracker. The high-level controller uses a model-based approach to determine the desired velocity and generate commands based on the robot's environment, while the low-level tracker ensures precise tracking of the desired commands while maintaining system stability. The system's adaptability is achieved through the dynamic calculation of desired velocities, allowing for real-time adjustments to ensure optimal robot movement. The proposed hierarchical control method has been successfully tested on the Cubot robot, demonstrating its effectiveness in navigating complex environments and adapting to changing conditions. The accompanying video showcases the robot's capabilities in traversing flat ground, stairs, and uneven terrain while achieving a high level of control accuracy. The source code for this project is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ethereaj/hierarchical_control. The video demonstrating the robot's capabilities is available on YouTube at https://youtu.be/7kqz2s0qzqA. In standard model checking, it is assumed that the structural information of a system is accurately known. However, this is not always the case in reality. Many systems are complex and hard to analyze, and as a result, their actual structure might deviate significantly from their intended or modeled structure. This paper addresses the challenge of model checking systems with uncertain or incomplete information. It proposes a measured version of CTL that allows for model checking on systems with known, uncertain measurements of structural elements, such as edges and vertices. This approach is applicable to systems represented as weighted graphs, where edge weights represent the reliability or certainty of edges. The paper presents an algorithm for verifying whether a given weighted graph satisfies a measured CTL specification, and also discusses its relationship with traditional CTL model checking. Furthermore, it provides a method for translating measured CTL specifications into standard CTL, making model checking more feasible. The paper also provides a concise proof of the equivalence between measured CTL verification and a specific type of linear programming. Finally, it highlights potential real-world applications of measured CTL model checking.

Our research introduces a groundbreaking early stopping rule for Krylov solvers within a specific framework of Interior Point Methods. This rule is founded on the observation that the residual norm can be overly conservative, leading to premature termination. In contrast, a more accurate measure of solution accuracy can be derived from the residual, along with a residual weighting scheme. Through rigorous analysis of linear systems arising from symmetric Positive Semi-Definite matrices, along with the application of the Collocation IP model, we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed termination criterion. In particular, we establish that the residual weighted by the cosine of its angle with the residual of the solution is both necessary and sufficient for determining convergence. In contrast, the traditional residual norm may be insufficient for convergence. In support of our analytical findings, we present numerical results confirming the superiority of our proposed criterion. In real-world applications, protecting personal information is a top priority, but the presence of identifying features can compromise privacy. Removing these features poses a challenge, as removing them altogether may result in unrecognizable images. Our approach focuses on individual re-identification reduction (IRR) where we aim to transform identities into clusters based on shared characteristics rather than distinct identities. Our innovative method, IIRCon, introduces a unique loss function and training strategy that leverages cluster-level feature alignment to preserve information while concealing identities. Compared to existing techniques, IIRCon yields superior results on two challenging datasets containing images and face data. Additionally, IIRCon's ability to preserve image quality and identify clusters makes it an attractive solution for applications where feature recognition is crucial. In the field of computer vision, deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the standard for numerous image classification tasks. However, the growing complexity and size of these models require them to be trained on expensive, specialized hardware, such as high-end GPUs, which can be difficult to access for researchers. To mitigate this issue, several studies have proposed domain migration techniques that enable trained models to be transferred to new, unfamiliar environments. This study evaluates the effectiveness of domain migration for image recognition tasks, using a standard dataset, and compares the performance of three migration approaches: 1) completely retraining the model from scratch, 2) fine-tuning it using transfer learning, and 3) using a method that adapts the model to the new environment without further training. The results show that the retraining approach and transfer learning perform similarly well, while other adaptation techniques can also be effective but are more sensitive to changes in the new environment. Interestingly, simply adjusting the model's input layer according to the new environment's data characteristics can lead to acceptable performance in many cases. Overall, the study suggests that the choice of migration method depends on the specific requirements of the new environment. In recent years, low-rank tensor regression has become increasingly significant due to its relevance in applications like signal processing, medical imaging, and climate science. However, existing optimization methods for LTR are often hindered by scalability issues, particularly in high dimensions. This research presents a novel algorithm, ISLET, which employs importance sampling to enhance the efficiency of LTR. By reformatting the regression problem into an optimization task and employing a sampling-based approach, ISLET offers a series of scalable and rapid solutions to LTR. We further demonstrate ISLET's superiority over existing methods, both theoretically and in real-world experiments. Notably, our results show that ISLET outperforms the state-of-the-art techniques, even in situations where important variables are correlated or uncorrelated. Additionally, our results highlight the effectiveness of ISLET in handling high-dimensional problems that are intractable for traditional methods. Overall, our research presents a groundbreaking tensor regression algorithm, ISLET, which offers impressive scalability and efficiency in tackling complex high-dimensional problems. Simulations of a galaxy collision involving equal-mass galaxies were conducted, 
with a focus on the effects of a dense, star-forming disk. These collisions 
resulted in the formation of a black hole through mergers of stars, which then 
induces active galactic nucleus outflows and subsequent star formation cessation 
due to gas expulsion. Notably, this expulsion has a more pronounced impact on lower 
mass galaxies with steeper density profiles. In contrast, collisions involving 
less massive galaxies with wider, less dense disks do not exhibit gas expulsion, 
ultimately leading to the formation of a disk galaxy with a flat rotation curve. 
A comparison of collision outcomes based on galaxy mass reveals distinct morphological 
differences, which are consistent with observed galaxy morphological types. 
Furthermore, simulations suggest that the star-formation cessation in the central 
region of a galaxy is a primary factor in determining its final galaxy type. 
Additionally, simulations of a single-galaxy collapse indicate that the formation 
of a disk galaxy is a likely outcome, which is in line with existing astrophysical 
models. In order to account for the observed distribution of galaxy types in the 
local universe, the star-formation cessation in the central region of a galaxy 
must occur at a rate of at least 50%. The results of this study are in line with 
existing observational evidence that the formation of a disk galaxy is a primary 
factor in determining galaxy type. However, a more complex collision involving 
unequal-mass galaxies will be explored in a subsequent study.

Link prediction is a crucial component of information extraction and network construction. Recent research has shown that connection learning can improve link forecasting by analyzing changes between entities. However, existing studies have been limited by their reliance on a single correlation type, such as co-occurrence or co-mentioning. To address this, we propose a novel framework called generalized connection learning that leverages multiple correlation types, such as semantic correlation. Our approach involves training a deep neural network to generate entity pairs based on these correlations. To facilitate this, we developed a cross-correlation recognition module that can detect correlations between entities or their attributes. Experimental results demonstrate that our generalized connection learning method outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in link forecasting, particularly in predicting evolving entities and relationships. Further analysis revealed that our method excels at predicting entities that rely on semantic correlations rather than co-occurrence or co-mentioning events. The accompanying code has been made publicly available. Notably, our work marks the first application of semantic correlation in connection learning and link forecasting. As a result, our method has the potential to significantly improve link forecasting accuracy and unlock new applications that rely on semantic correlation. Using Saito's residuum of a logarithmic vector bundle, we establish a direct method to determine the isomorphism classes of regular meromorphic differential structures on a projective variety. This approach bypasses the need for explicit local parameters at risk, offering a significantly streamlined calculation. The method is effectively applied to investigate structures associated with weighted homogeneous vector bundles. Furthermore, we leverage this technique to discover novel integrable differential equations arising in moduli spaces, and provide a concise, inductive method for constructing integrable logarithmic vector bundles. The validity of our approach is reinforced by examining specific examples, such as the moduli space of vector bundles of rank two on $\mathbb{P}^1$, and the moduli space of line bundles on a curve. Notably, the latter yields an integrable differential equation on the universal vector bundle over the Kummer surface derived from a tetragonal curve. The method is also extended to study integrable differential equations in the context of quasihomogeneous vector bundles. This yields a comprehensive understanding of the integrable structures on the moduli spaces of quasihomogeneous vector bundles over a curve, and the universal vector bundle on K3 surfaces arising from tetragonal covers. The validity of our approach is further confirmed by examining specific examples, such as the universal vector bundle on the Kummer surface, and the universal bundle on a surface obtained from a tetragonal cover. The paper concludes by outlining potential avenues for future research. The accompanying code, written in the SageMath programming language, is included as supplementary material. Classical simulations of quantum circuits can be hindered by a significant overhead in execution time. A method to minimize this burden is to compile the quantum circuits into more efficient forms. This paper introduces a new approach to recompile quantum circuits using Clifford gates, which can lead to a substantial decrease in their circuit depth. By utilizing a novel non-clifford gate decomposition technique combined with a Clifford circuit peeling method, the paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach. Experimental results show that this method can achieve a speedup of up to 3.6 for specific quantum circuits, such as the ZQC and RICC circuits, and an average speedup of 2.1 for a set of randomly generated circuits. This method can be applied to any quantum circuit and may yield even greater speedups for more complex circuits. The implementation of this approach is available on GitHub. This paper also provides a critical analysis of the limitations of the current Clifford compilation method and suggests future research directions. The findings of this paper are expected to contribute to the development of more efficient classical simulations of quantum circuits. In a decentralized manner, Federated Learning (FL) enables the training of machine learning models on a large number of mobile devices, or in this case, vehicular edge units, where data is safeguarded against a central server by remaining locally stored on device. However, the limited resources, such as processing power, storage, and communication, of mobile edge units pose a significant challenge to the conventional FL approach. To address these issues, we propose a highly mobile, low-latency, and efficient VE-FL framework. This framework leverages a multi-vehicle, multi-lane setup to enable the creation of a virtual and densely connected edge cluster. This allows for the efficient aggregation of local models, while minimizing data transmission between the local devices and a central server using a novel, in-cluster data aggregation method. Additionally, we implement an adaptive, vehicle-to-vehicle data transmission protocol that adjusts to changing network conditions. Our proposed framework is evaluated using real-world data from a large-scale highway in the United States, yielding a 2.5 times improvement in model accuracy over conventional FL methods. Moreover, the proposed approach results in a 70% reduction in the number of transmitted bits and a 40% decrease in the number of transmitted model versions compared to state-of-the-art solutions. This novel FL framework is poised to empower a wide range of applications in smart transportation, including autonomous driving, smart toll collection, and traffic management systems. Furthermore, the framework's adaptability and scalability enable it to be easily extended to other mobile edge applications beyond transportation, including smart grids and mobile health systems. Our results demonstrate the potential of this framework to unlock new possibilities in the field of mobile edge computing. Code for the proposed framework is available on GitHub. This article provides detailed descriptions of Lie group structures based on 2-stage nilpotent Lie algebras, including an alternative proof that dual Lie algebras yield dual group structures. We also develop explicit geometric representations for the Lie groups corresponding to 2-step nilpotent Lie algebras of real dimension $2n$, specifically through $\mathbb{R}^{2n+1}$-symmetric Riemannian manifolds. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these geometric representations are unique when considering a given Lie algebra up to diffeomorphisms and measure multiplications. As an application, we establish a geometric characterization of the leaf space of a specific foliation derived from a particular distribution, induced by a nilpotent double extension of a 2-step nilpotent Lie algebra. Lastly, we establish a criterion based on the exponential map's image for a Lie algebra to be derived from a complete, connected Lie group. A location-based service (LBS) is a mobile service that utilizes location information (LI) to offer various functions, such as providing emergency assistance and promoting local businesses. However, providing LBS requires users to share their LI with service providers, which raises significant privacy concerns. To address these concerns, a proposed LBS protocol utilizes edge computing (EC) to safeguard user privacy. By leveraging EC, this protocol enables devices to transmit LI to nearby edge nodes, which then forward the information to LBS servers without revealing the user's identity. Additionally, edge nodes are capable of redirecting requests to nearby nodes, effectively concealing the user's LI from adjacent devices. By integrating a game theory-based approach, this mechanism is able to determine the optimal edge nodes for each user, while minimizing the time it takes for LI to reach LBS servers. Experimental results demonstrate that this protocol significantly reduces LI exposure and achieves substantial energy savings, reaching up to 80% and 90% respectively, in comparison to existing protocols. A further analysis of the protocol's performance under varying network conditions, including noise and fading, indicates that it is capable of sustaining a 10% improvement in energy savings. Ultimately, this protocol offers a promising solution for providing LBS while maintaining user privacy. Future research directions involve exploring the use of blockchain technology to further enhance the protocol's security and efficiency. A graph's perfect matching is referred to as a flawless pairing, and a subset of its edges forms a path if there's no shared edge between consecutive points. In this study, we examine the problem of determining if a given graph has a matching where no two selected edges belong to the same path, and we consider specific cases where the graph's vertices are grouped into categories. In medical imaging, domain adaptation plays a vital role in overcoming the limitations of limited training data availability. A primary challenge medical imaging researchers often face is limited data, leading to biased models. Our research aims to address this issue by proposing an innovative unsupervised domain adaptation approach that enables models to learn domain-invariant features from limited data. This method utilizes graph convolutional networks to isolate sample-specific features from domain-specific features, allowing for more accurate transfer learning. Our proposed method demonstrates significant performance improvements in various benchmark datasets, achieving state-of-the-art results in some cases. Our method's effectiveness is particularly evident in medical image classification tasks, such as categorizing brain tumors and breast lesions, and achieving competitive performance on the NIH Stroke Network Atlas (NSNAT) challenge. This approach's source-free domain adaptation capability makes it an ideal solution for real-world clinical applications. The source-free domain adaptation approach has the potential to overcome the limitations of limited data, thereby facilitating more accurate and reliable medical image classification. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through simulated experiments involving both simple and challenging scenarios. Ultimately, this work aims to illuminate the underlying principles of active inference and make it more accessible to researchers studying reinforcement learning. A binary word $w$ is classified as a Gray code if it differs from the previous word $w'$ by either a single position flip or a change of leading $k$ bits from $0$ to $1$, where $k$ is less than or equal to the length of the word.  The intersection of two binary words $w$ and $w'$ is defined as the concatenation of their common bits, and a sequence of binary words is considered an intersection cycle if each subsequent term shares a common part with the preceding term.  In this research, we investigate the existence of specific intersection cycles for particular types of binary words that are constrained to have a limited number of $1$'s or $0$'s.  In particular, we demonstrate that for binary words with at most $2$ occurrences of $1$ or $0$, every initial segment of an increasing sequence of words with at most $2$ occurrences of $1$ or $0$ will eventually form a cycle.  Additionally, we show that for binary words with at most $3$ occurrences of $1$ or $0$, every intersection cycle of length $5$ or less is also a Gray code.  However, we also find counterexamples for both claims when the constraint on the number of $1$ or $0$ occurrences is increased.  Finally, we outline several unresolved questions regarding intersection cycles and Gray codes.  In particular, we demonstrate that there exists a binary word with at most $3$ occurrences of $1$ or $0$ that does not have any cycles of length $5$ or less, and we conjecture that there exists a Gray code of length $12$ that is not an intersection cycle.  Additionally, we show that for binary words with at most $3$ occurrences of $1$ or $0$, every intersection cycle of length $12$ or less is also a Gray code, but we do not have a similar result for longer cycles. fluctuating scales and intense, yet intermittant, spatial patterns that are
perceptible only over time frames that are longer than the system's natural
cycling periods. The unpredictability arises from the interplay between the
inherent dynamics of the system and the limitations imposed by the available
information. This paper introduces a model-free, data-driven approach to
predict the future behavior of turbulent systems, which leverages the
information available in past observations. The proposed method is applied to the
Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, a well-established model for spatio-temporally
turbulent systems, and demonstrates its ability to make accurate predictions
even when only a small portion of the system's behavior is perceivable over short
time frames. The underlying mechanism of this method is analyzed, and it is
found that it can be approximated by a specific class of deep neural networks.

range of turbulent systems, including those that are subject to external noise. The
flexibility of the method is further showcased by its ability to be trained using
data from a related, yet distinct, turbulent system. The proposed method is also
compared to existing approaches, and it is shown that it can achieve comparable
performance using significantly less data and fewer model parameters. Overall, the
results suggest that the proposed method is a promising direction for accurately

In point cloud processing, data reduction through resampling is a common approach. Despite its potential, overly aggressive resampling can lead to significant losses in detail and even break down reconstruction. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel hypergraph-based method that leverages the inherent structure of point clouds. By representing points as hypergraph vertices and utilizing geometric distances as edges, this method constructs an interconnected network. By solving an optimization problem on this hypergraph, we achieve resampled points that maintain their original shape's integrity. In addition, we propose a refined method that incorporates edge weights, noise sensitivity, and geometric continuity to produce high-quality resampled point clouds. Through extensive experiments, our approach has demonstrated superior performance in preserving details and geometric structure compared to existing methods. Our method is based on the observation that certain grammatical mistakes are more prevalent than others. Building on this insight, we categorize 14 common error types into significant and common errors, developing a hybrid model that combines supervised learning with common error modeling. Our approach outperforms the baseline in 10 out of 15 assessments, achieving an overall improvement of 4.1 points on AccuScore, or 7.3%. Additionally, our model surpasses or matches the performance of the current best system in all evaluations. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that our model excels at recognizing common errors, which are indeed prevalent in the data. Future directions for research on the topic are also discussed. By leveraging the groups, cosmologists can derive valuable information about the universe's matter density and the nature of its dark energy component. Despite their utility, galaxy groups face significant challenges stemming from systematic uncertainties. To address these issues, this study examines the impact of various uncertainties on the cosmological parameters derived from galaxy groups, specifically focusing on the richness of the halo, the selection function, the galaxy luminosity function, and the K-correction. By employing a mock catalog of the BOSS DR12 spectroscopic survey and a mock galaxy catalog, the study assesses the effect of these uncertainties on the recovered cosmological parameters. Furthermore, the study reveals that the K-correction uncertainty yields a correlation with the uncertainty in the selection function, suggesting that the two should be considered together when studying galaxy groups. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that the cosmological parameters derived from galaxy groups are relatively insensitive to the selection function, a promising characteristic for their use in future cosmological studies. The primary objective of this study is to verify whether long-period transit events occur in the spectra of stars classified as {\delta} Sct variables. We conducted a detailed examination of Kepler light curves from 110 {\delta} Sct stars. Our analysis revealed that 12 of these stars exhibit characteristics consistent with transit phenomena, with most transit events having amplitudes exceeding 0.1 {\rm mag}. Upon closer inspection, the transit signals in six stars could be attributed to eclipsing binary systems, with the remaining six stars displaying transit signatures unattributable to known eclipsing binary counterparts. Given the significant radial velocity amplitude of {\delta} Sct variables, the transit signals in these six stars may be indicative of the presence of a (slowly spinning) transiting companion, possibly a brown dwarf or a low-mass main-sequence companion, or a close-in, cool, and low-mass companion, such as an M dwarf or an early red dwarf. Alternatively, the transit signals could be due to the presence of a circumstellar disk, such as a debris disk or a protoplanetary disk, or to other phenomena like the presence of a circumbinary disk or a close-in Jupiter-mass planet. Further investigation, including spectroscopic analysis, is necessary to determine the nature of the transit events observed in these six {\delta} Sct stars. This study has the potential to shed light on the phenomenon of transit events observed in {\delta} Sct variables. We have also developed a method for detecting transit events in the light curves of {\delta} Sct variables, which can be applied to other types of variable stars. Furthermore, the study provides a list of potential candidates for transit events observable with the upcoming {\em TESS} mission. We have also identified a subset of {\delta} Sct variables that are likely to host transiting companions, with the possibility of some of these companions being in the M-dwarf mass range. This paper outlines a framework for mitigating congestion in ground transportation systems, particularly at hubs like John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City. The proposed solution involves adjusting existing bus arrival times, taking into account factors such as traffic flow, road conditions, and traffic lights. This approach is implemented using a modified version of the cell transmission model, which simulates traffic flow and incorporates a queueing theory-based model to account for traffic lights. The proposed framework is applied to JFK, where it successfully reduces overall travel time for passengers by an average of 18% to 20%. The study also highlights potential limitations and suggests future improvements to the model. The way people visually analyze and process information differs significantly from how computers analyze and process information through algorithms. While computers are limited by strict rules and algorithms, humans bring personal experiences, prior knowledge, and biases to their observations. This human aspect often leads to inconsistent conclusions when examining the same data with a computer. This study aims to understand how setting a time limit affects human-computer differences in visual inspection. A photo analysis task was designed, where participants were asked to identify a specific object, either with or without a time constraint. Our findings show that introducing a time constraint significantly enhances object detection accuracy for humans but has a negligible impact on computers. Moreover, we found that adding a time constraint during the analysis phase shifts human focus from the bigger picture to individual objects, increasing object detection accuracy. Interestingly, despite improved object detection accuracy, humans still tend to disagree with computers when focusing on individual frames, highlighting the potential for developing more human-centered AI systems that take into account human visual preferences. Our study's findings have the potential to improve AI performance by incorporating human insights. In the United States, voters frequently engage in face-to-face discussions about politics, particularly during election seasons, which can be attributed to the country's decentralized and non-mandatory party system. Despite the importance of interpersonal political conversations, there has been a lack of research on how these interactions shape voter preferences and voting habits. Our study leverages a large dataset of over 3 million in-person conversations between voters at Iowa caucuses between 2016 and 2020. We analyze how these conversations influence an individual's perception of their chosen candidate by examining the impact of a voter engaging with someone who strongly supports a rival candidate. Our results indicate that a voter's likelihood of switching support to a rival candidate increases when interacting with someone who strongly supports that candidate. However, this effect is absent when the rival candidate is less prominent. Our study also finds that a voter's political ideology and pre-existing party loyalty mitigate the influence of conversations on their decision-making. These findings suggest that private political discussions can significantly influence voter behavior, which can be a crucial factor in shaping election outcomes. Our study's results can be applied to elections in countries with multi-party systems to help identify areas where in-person conversations may be more effective in inducing changes in voting behavior. Ultimately, this research underscores the importance of creating a culture that encourages open and constructive dialogue between individuals with differing viewpoints. By doing so, we may be able to reduce the polarization and animosity often associated with politics and promote a more democratic society. A new approach called the Cuckoo Filter has been developed for fast membership testing in probabilistic data structures. It is composed of a nested sequence of cuckoo bins and a backing memory store. To determine a query's membership, it involves checking if the backing store contains the associated data, with each element in bins is filled at a certain probability. In this paper, we introduce two new Cuckoo Filter variants that can adapt to varying capacities. The first one dynamically adjusts its capacity based on the number of elements stored, while the second one fixes it in relation to the input size. Both variants utilize a new concept called support efficiency, which measures the ratio of backing-store elements to the average capacity of the nested bins. We found that the first variant is more suitable when the support efficiency is high, while the second one is more suitable when the support efficiency is low. In deep learning models, especially those used for educational purposes, it is often necessary to have multiple outputs. For example, a model designed to predict the probability of a student being on task and the corresponding learning gain over time would require multiple outputs. However, training such models proves to be more complicated than those with a single output. One major challenge is that multiple output models are often non-differentiable and therefore difficult to optimize. To address this issue, we propose a novel optimization method that allows for the efficient training of deep educational models with multiple outputs. By breaking down the training process into smaller steps and using a differentiable loss function, our approach enables the seamless backpropagation of errors. In our method, each output is associated with a specific equivalence relation, which is then used to minimize the loss function in a stepwise manner. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by testing it on two educational datasets and show that it outperforms existing methods, such as multi-task learning and weight sharing, by achieving superior performance in terms of accuracy, F1 score, and learning gain. Our results suggest that this new approach is a promising direction for the development of deep educational models. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications of this method in the context of educational technology. Code for the implementation of our approach is available on GitHub. To enhance semi-supervised learning, particularly for computer vision tasks, we propose an innovative approach called FlexMatch. FlexMatch leverages a curriculum-based method of pseudo label tagging to refine model training. It achieves this by dynamically adjusting the difficulty of samples through a joint consideration of samples' confidence and loss magnitude. In this manner, the approach ensures a more effective and efficient use of unlabeled samples for model improvement. To further optimize the pseudo labeling process, we have developed a new loss function called P4. When paired with our pseudo tagging strategy, P4 loss helps to minimize the issue of ambiguity in unlabeled samples, thereby guiding the model towards more accurate results. Experimental results demonstrate FlexMatch's ability to achieve significant improvements over current methods, with notable increases in accuracy on object detection tasks. In particular, the approach has shown remarkable results on the COCO dataset, achieving 49.5% mAP using a single GPU, and 50.4% mAP when utilizing four GPUs. Additionally, the code for FlexMatch is made publicly available on the GitHub repository FlexMatch.

A novel approach to training deep neural networks on a large scale, known as federated learning, has emerged as a way to safeguard user data. Despite its benefits, traditional methods often rely on a single 'world model' that's updated using data from various users, which can lead to suboptimal outcomes due to differing data distributions among users. In response, a new 'client-centric' approach has been developed, in which each client updates their model independently using data from their own environment. However, this approach often results in models becoming too specialized to their local data and failing to generalize well. In an effort to overcome this limitation, a new training method called 'customized federated training' has been proposed, which leverages hypernetworks to create client models that are adaptable to changing data environments. By combining hypernetworks with federated learning, it's possible to balance specialization and generalization, resulting in better overall performance. In experiments involving various tasks, the proposed method outperformed traditional methods in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. For instance, in a benchmark test, the proposed method achieved 2.9% higher accuracy on CIFAR-10 compared to a baseline approach. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrated its ability to adapt to new environments by successfully transferring knowledge from a source environment to a target environment. Overall, the proposed method offers a promising solution for large-scale federated learning applications. The versatility of transformer-based language models, particularly multilingual BERT (mBERT), has been observed in its ability to perform well in low-resource settings. This study investigates the pretraining process of mBERT by analyzing its transferability to new languages through a two-step approach. We first utilize mBERT to translate target language word embeddings, then refine them using a simple linear layer. Following this, we use the refined embeddings to predict the sequence of a target language under highly challenging conditions. Results indicate that mBERT's ability to generalize to new languages is largely driven by its language detection capabilities during the translation phase. Interestingly, when the language is identified correctly, mBERT exhibits impressive language modeling capabilities, enabling accurate sequence prediction. However, when the language is misidentified, mBERT's language modeling capabilities are severely impaired. These findings suggest that the language detection capabilities of mBERT during the pretraining process are critical in understanding its ability to generalize to new languages. Moreover, we find that mBERT's language detection capabilities are inherently linked to its language modeling capabilities. As a result, we propose that the language detection process should be considered as a critical component of mBERT's language modeling capabilities. To facilitate this understanding, we propose a new framework for analyzing the language detection capabilities of mBERT. We also demonstrate that mBERT's language detection capabilities are not limited to language identification, but can be extended to include a range of related tasks, such as language classification, word alignment, and sentence alignment. Finally, we show that mBERT's language detection capabilities can be leveraged to develop a range of language transfer tasks, including word translation, sentence alignment, and document alignment. Overall, this study highlights the importance of language detection capabilities in language modeling and suggests that the language detection process should be considered as a critical component of mBERT's language modeling capabilities. It also provides a framework for analyzing the language detection capabilities of mBERT and highlights the potential of mBERT in language transfer tasks. To improve the efficiency of convergence to geometric convergence for the power iteration method in updating the eigenvector for the preconditioned eigenvalue problem, a gradient descent method is proposed. By minimizing a cost function that measures the distance between the projected vector and the actual eigenvector, this approach aims to accelerate convergence and achieve self-adaptive properties. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed gradient descent method can indeed achieve geometric convergence and offers improved convergence rates compared to the standard power iteration approach. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the gradient descent method can be applied to Ritz vector selection and has the potential to result in faster convergence rates. The findings also indicate that the efficacy of the gradient descent method depends on the distribution of the preconditioned eigenvalues. In particular, our results show that the method excels when the largest Ritz vector corresponds to the largest eigenvalue associated with the smallest eigenvalue in the eigenvalue spectrum. In addition, our research explores the interplay between geometric convergence and the stability of the preconditioning process. In the context of the Helmholtz equation, our numerical analysis reveals that the method is particularly effective when the imaginary part of the complex eigenvalue is large. In contrast, our results show that the method is more effective when the imaginary part is small when the preconditioner is complex. This review explores the theoretical and numerical development of cosmic dynamo theory, tracing its history and evolution from its beginnings in the 1950s to the present. The article begins with an overview of dynamo fundamentals, describes the classic vector mean method for generating large-scale magnetic fields, and examines the main components of cosmic dynamo theory, including small-scale and large-scale dynamos, alpha-effect, and mean-field models. It then examines key advancements in dynamo theory, including the kinematic dynamo theorem, the anisotropic kinematic dynamo, and the direct dynamo theorem, and discusses how these concepts have been applied to astrophysical and geophysical phenomena, such as galactic and solar dynamos, convection dynamos, and geodynamo. The article also discusses the direct numerical simulation of astrophysical dynamos, from molecular clouds to active galactic nuclei, and the challenges and uncertainties in these simulations, as well as the direct dynamo theorem's implications for understanding astrophysical objects. The article concludes with an overview of recent research and future challenges and opportunities in the study of cosmic dynamos. To address this issue, we propose a novel framework that leverages both content information and user biases to enhance the representation of items with text descriptions. Our approach involves two primary components: a biased model that incorporates user biases into item latent encodings and a biased loss function that prioritizes items with relevant user biases. Experimental results on two benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework in improving recommendation accuracy and item diversity. Research output evaluation heavily relies on citation analysis, with its most prominent metric being the h-index, which calculates an author's distinct publications, aiming to balance their influence and quantity. However, this metric has a limitation in accounting for collaborative research, where multiple publications are contributed by diverse authors, resulting in an underestimation of an author's overall influence due to shared citations. This issue can be addressed by considering an author's full body of work and incorporating collaboration into the evaluation, which could involve redefining the h-index or developing alternative metrics, such as those based on author-count or influence-weighted publications, to provide a more comprehensive view of an author's contributions. By doing so, researchers can more accurately assess an author's impact, including their collaborative efforts, and gain insights into potential new metrics, not least through the development of a software tool that calculates these values. We propose a novel task called Query Entailment, which necessitates a model's ability to verify the justification behind a query and express it in a sequence of interconnected reasoning steps that accurately corresponds to its own reasoning process. This task is particularly relevant in the context of Question Answering, where users have the option to query the model for explanations of its answers, and it is essential for the explanations to be authentic and truthful. To achieve this goal, we present a method for generating a sequence of interconnected reasoning steps that mirrors the model's internal reasoning process and propose a ranking-based approach to select a sequence that accurately justifies the query. The effectiveness of this approach is evaluated on the HANS dataset, which reveals that our method excels in generating genuine explanations for queries with clear and straightforward justification steps. Furthermore, by adapting our entailing model to a zero-shot setting, we achieve substantial improvements in both the accuracy of accurate explanations and the detection of fabricated justifications, as evidenced by our results on the HANS dataset. A comprehensive search of radio sources in the Green Bank Telescope 43-meter database was conducted to identify potential pulsars and radio bursts. The search focused on 1,000 sources with radio luminosity exceeding 10^44 erg per second, discovered between 1955 and 1962. The search area included a 1-degree square region surrounding each source, with observations made at 144 MHz with a 10-second integration time. The results revealed 12 pulsar candidates, of which 3 were confirmed and 9 remained uncertain. The confirmed pulsars included one millisecond and two young pulsars. This paper introduces the Hidden Space Conditioning on Generative Confrontational Networks (HSCGCN) method for conditional image generation. A hidden space is created by combining latent vectors from a conditional input and a random vector, which is then encoded into a latent representation via a multi-layer perceptron. The generated image can be modified by adjusting the hidden space's weight vector. This approach enables the incorporation of multiple conditional inputs and allows for the analysis of interactions between inputs. Furthermore, a novel technique called disentangled confrontation is proposed, which separates the input's influence on the hidden space into two distinct components. The first component modifies the image's overall content, while the second alters specific features without affecting others. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of HSCCN in generating images with distinct features and reveal insights into the relationships between inputs and generated outputs. The rapid growth of IoT devices has led to a surge in offloading tasks to nearby edge servers, with cloud computing still struggling to meet the demands of resource-constrained devices. Despite the potential of edge server offloading, current offloading systems lack a key feature: allowing users to have complete control over their tasks and data. This limitation hinders the effectiveness of existing systems, which often rely on third-party cloud servers to offload tasks. Our research introduces Self-Managed IoT (SMIoT), a system that empowers users to manage their local edge server for task offloading, ensuring full user authority over their data. By enabling users to decide which tasks to offload, when to offload, and to which server, SMIoT provides a more practical and personalized offloading solution. Our experiments demonstrate that SMIoT significantly outperforms existing systems in terms of task success rates, average task completion time, and average data transmission. Our results show that SMIoT achieves a 98.5% task success rate, a 1.9x reduction in average task completion time, and a 2.5x reduction in average data transmission compared to the best existing system. Furthermore, we've found that the accuracy of our estimates improves when considering longer time windows. Our research also reveals that the choice of prior distribution has a greater impact on the estimation of drift coefficients, as opposed to diffusion coefficients. To validate our approach, we've conducted a series of Monte Carlo simulations and compared the performance of our method with other popular methods, including maximum likelihood estimation and the Bayesian approach with a Gaussian prior. While maximum likelihood estimation performed well for large datasets, the Bayesian approach demonstrated superior results, particularly when working with limited data. Leveraging the same Bayesian approach, we've also successfully reconstructed the underlying dynamics of a large dataset of human mobility data. Our results show that the estimated reproduction numbers are highly sensitive to the choice of prior distribution, but the Bayesian approach provides more accurate estimates, particularly when working with limited data. The goal of Visual Inquiry Answering (VIAA) involves generating answers based on the context of a given image. Current neural-based VIAA systems excel in evaluating simple queries but struggle when answering more complex ones, which necessitates the model to grasp the context of the question. To address this limitation, a new domain generalization approach for VIAA is proposed. This method, referred to as Enhanced RAMEN, utilizes a combination of a pre-trained language model and a memory component to facilitate the model's understanding of the context. To further improve the model's performance, a novel loss function is introduced that incorporates a contrastive learning component. Experimental results demonstrate Enhanced RAMEN's effectiveness in enhancing the model's performance on more complex queries. Additionally, the model's performance in processing queries from unseen domains is found to be superior to existing state-of-the-art VIAA systems. Recent approaches have primarily focused on developing video-specific frameworks that utilize temporal information to achieve better recognition results. Conversely, this paper advocates for an alternative strategy: leveraging vision-language models to facilitate video recognition. This research delves into sequence forecasting techniques for Arabic text with varied scripts, which is a complex problem requiring advanced methods. We introduce a novel multi-task sequence prediction framework that simultaneously forecasts multiple outputs: the predicted sequence, its likelihood, and likelihood breakdown for each step. We implement this approach on the Tunisian Arabic dialect and demonstrate its effectiveness through a new dataset and evaluation metric. We further examine the challenges posed by Arabic script variations and propose a solution to mitigate them. Finally, we showcase the performance of our method and compare it to single-task sequence prediction and a multi-task sequence forecasting baseline incorporating Arabic script modifications. In reinforcement learning, tampering with rewards is a critical concern that can severely impact policy training, particularly in environments where agents are human-driven. This research examines the effects of reward tampering on the learned policy, focusing on the perspectives of both the agent itself and the entities influencing rewards. We analyze how different types of reward tampering, such as when humans intentionally alter rewards, affect the learning process and propose a framework to address these issues. This framework is demonstrated through a set of case studies, and we also explore potential remedies to mitigate the negative consequences of reward tampering. Ultimately, this research aims to provide a clear understanding of the effects of reward tampering on reinforcement learning. 

This research is significant because it addresses the limitations of current reinforcement learning research, which often neglects reward tampering. Furthermore, the paper highlights the need for a formal and causal analysis of the impact of reward tampering, which is critical for understanding its effects. We believe that this research will inspire further investigation into the role of rewards in reinforcement learning and help to establish a more comprehensive understanding of the underlying dynamics involved.

Our research explores the properties of context-free grammars with selection rules drawn from LTL2, a logic that allows us to express context-free languages with increased flexibility. Building on this logic, we developed a new class, rll2, by incorporating a restriction, called rigidity, which prevents shifting the focus while maintaining equivalence to context-free languages. Notably, rll2 significantly expands the possibilities of context-free language creation, surpassing the capabilities of LTL2. In fact, rll2 allows the construction of a substantial number of context-free languages that cannot be generated by LTL2. This discovery highlights the creative potential of context-free grammars with the specific type of selection rules defined by rll2. Our findings are grounded in a newly developed translation from LTL2 to a system of regular expressions, which we call LTL2reg, and a specific property of LTL2reg that we call the disjunction property. Building on this translation, we prove that rll2 is more powerful than LTL2 by constructing a specific context-free language that cannot be generated by LTL2. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of rll2 through a series of examples, including the creation of a parser for JSON and a lexer for a programming language. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our research, specifically the potential to create more expressive formalisms by incorporating the rigidity constraint. Additionally, we examine the relationship between rll2 and other advanced formalisms, such as the tree automata model, and explore the potential for future research in this area. In the field of system performance modeling, researchers have been studying load distribution models for many years. These models typically involve complex stochastic processes, often with nonlinear dynamics, and are challenging to analyze directly. However, recent advancements have led to the development of novel methods for examining stochastic processes, such as using doubly exponential sums to quantify system performance. This approach has proven to be highly effective in analyzing a wide range of performance models, including Markovian arrival processes and phase-type service times. In this study, we demonstrate that the doubly exponential sum can be used to represent the performance of load distribution models, even when they are driven by more complex stochastic processes, provided that the service times can be represented as a time-reversible Markovian arrival process. Furthermore, we show that the doubly exponential sum can be represented as a stationary time series, and we derive a closed-form expression for the autocovariance function of this series. This result enables us to establish a connection between the doubly exponential sum and the stationary time series, and we demonstrate that the former can be approximated using empirical distributions of the latter. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations, which demonstrate the applicability of the doubly exponential sum in analyzing load distribution models. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive review of the existing literature on doubly exponential sums and their applications in performance modeling. This work is the first to explore the use of doubly exponential sums in load distribution models, and we believe that this approach will be highly beneficial for researchers studying stochastic processes, system performance modeling, and applied probability. In fact, we envision that the doubly exponential sum can be used to represent a wide range of performance models, and we believe that the method will be highly valuable for practitioners working in these fields. In support of our research, we have developed a Python package, called pyde, which can be used to analyze and approximate the behavior of the doubly exponential sum. This package is available at https://github.com/zharkov/doubly-expo. In addition, we have developed a companion R package, called deanalyzer, which can be used to analyze and estimate the behavior of the doubly exponential sum. This package is available at https://cran.r-project.org/package=deanalyzer. Both packages are available under the terms of the GPL v3. We hope that these tools will be highly beneficial for researchers studying performance modeling and applied probability. Individuals typically rely on external tools like to-do lists, calendars, and notebooks to manage tasks and tasks-related activities. However, the actual time spent on these tasks remains recorded in personal devices like mobile phones, laptops, and work systems, including calendars and time-tracking software. This study aims to understand how individuals integrate work activities into their calendars, which is crucial for accurately calculating time spent on tasks. We conducted a study by providing participants with a month-long tracking using Google Calendar, and we found that: (1) they record time spent on activities more than three times more than task lists, (2) most activities are not scheduled with a specific time, and (3) many tasks involve recurring activities. Based on these results, we propose an approach to estimate time spent on tasks by analyzing changes in calendar entries. Experimental results show that this approach can produce accurate estimates. Furthermore, we discovered that integrating calendar data with time-tracking systems can provide more detailed insights into user behavior, enabling the creation of a comprehensive picture of task-related activities. This study contributes to the development of task management systems that can accurately track time spent on tasks. All data and code used in the study have been made publicly available. In high-energy physics research, accurately mapping event data is a significant challenge. Recent studies have shown that graph neural networks can efficiently tackle this issue, but their training time is substantial and their models are often resource-intensive. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes an innovative approach that deploys graph neural networks in a highly parallel manner across field-programmable gate arrays, significantly reducing processing time while maintaining a compact model size. The proposed deployment of proximity-weighted graph neural networks in FPGA systems has been successfully implemented and demonstrated, achieving a 2-4 times improvement in processing speed while maintaining a comparable model size. The performance of this deployment was evaluated using data from the Large Hadron Collider, and it was found to achieve comparable accuracy to traditional methods while processing data instantly. The proposed deployment was also found to be highly adaptable, easily integrating with existing computing infrastructure without requiring significant upgrades. This study's findings open up new possibilities for using graph neural networks in various high-performance applications, and its results have significant implications for future research in high-energy physics and beyond. The source code for this deployment is publicly available on the GitHub repository "PW-GNN-on-FPGA".

Reinforcement learning has been instrumental in developing intelligent agents that excel at decision-making in complex environments. However, the traditional reinforcement learning framework assumes a static environment, which is often far from the truth. In reality, environmental dynamics, such as seasonal changes, can have a profound impact on agent performance. To address this, we propose a temporal change reinforcement learning (TCRL) framework, which leverages change detection and multi-task reinforcement learning techniques to ensure agents can adapt to evolving environments. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments in both grid-world and simulated urban traffic scenarios. Our findings indicate that incorporating change detection and multi-task reinforcement learning capabilities enables agents to quickly adapt to changes, even if they are rare, and suggests a promising approach for operating autonomous robots and vehicles across diverse and dynamic contexts. Energy grid models are typically represented by nonlinear differential-algebraic equations, which pose significant challenges for numerical solutions. The associated root problem is notoriously difficult to solve accurately and efficiently. In this research, we develop a novel method to assess the state of energy grids by leveraging the properties of the underlying differential-algebraic equations. This approach involves analyzing the behavior of the Jacobian matrix and incorporating a preconditioned Krylov subspace method, which also requires an initial approximation. We introduce a specific strategy for generating an initial guess from a reduced nonlinear model, and demonstrate its efficacy through numerical experiments with real-world examples. The results show that this approach can quickly determine whether a stable equilibrium solution exists and can identify any deviations from this state. Furthermore, we find that the preconditioned Krylov subspace method can converge to the actual solution for many power grid models, even when initial approximations are far from the equilibrium point. The numerical experiments also highlight the importance of careful preconditioning and scaling, as well as the ability of the proposed method to adapt to different types of power grid models. We introduce a novel, automated system for object handling known as particle-driven object handling (POH). Unlike conventional methods, POH empowers robots to grasp and manipulate irregularly shaped objects without prior knowledge of their form or structure. This breakthrough is achieved through the use of a cutting-edge algorithm that generates a set of collision-free trajectories in real-time, taking into account an object's geometric properties and contact points. By generating a set of potential trajectories, POH enables robots to adaptively select the most effective approach, thereby enhancing robustness and effectiveness. POH's ability to operate autonomously, process complex object shapes, and achieve high success rates makes it an attractive solution for a wide range of object handling applications. POH's effectiveness has been successfully demonstrated in a range of challenging object handling tasks, including object picking and placement, object manipulation, and insertion. As shown by the experimental results, POH's ability to operate autonomously and generate multiple trajectories in real-time significantly improves overall success rates and enables robots to adapt to unexpected object shapes. POH's potential applications extend to a broad range of domains, including robotic assembly, robotic manipulation, and robotic placement. The Go programming language has become increasingly popular for creating concurrent applications.  However, identifying the sources of concurrency issues can be complicated due to Go's unique blend of high-level and low-level features.  Our research presents BinGo, a tool that analyzes Go executables to pinpoint potential concurrency problems.  When users compile Go programs into executables, BinGo identifies key data structures, such as locks and queues, and maps the program's control flow and functionality to these structures.  This information helps BinGo detect five common concurrency issues and provide detailed diagnostics.  Through testing, we found that BinGo accurately diagnosed concurrency issues in numerous open-source projects and successfully identified issues in several well-known projects on GitHub, including a previously unidentified problem in the Rev reverse software.  Our results demonstrate that BinGo can effectively identify concurrency flaws in Go programs independent of the language's underlying source code.  Our tool and accompanying source code are freely available at https://github.com/secure-systems-lab/go-concurrency-inspector.  A video outlining the tool is accessible at https://youtu.be/7cQs2qzqzqA.  The Go community has incorporated elements of BinGo into the Go static analyzer, including a lock checker. Hyperspectral images play a significant role in remote sensing and environmental monitoring, yet their utility is severely hindered by noise, leading to suboptimal results. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel model called SSCAN that effectively leverages both spatial and spectral information to remove noise from hyperspectral images. By employing a unique attention-based mechanism, SSCAN selectively weighs the importance of spatial and spectral data to produce a denoised image. Our model's ability to accurately restore hyperspectral images is demonstrated through extensive experiments on various datasets, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods in terms of both quantitative metrics and visual quality. Furthermore, SSCAN's efficiency and adaptability are established through its successful deployment on a diverse range of hyperspectral images. The task of registering multiple images in a single scene, with varying viewpoints and orientations, is a complex problem. Existing methods that rely on a single, continuous viewing graph are not effective in accurately registering images in such scenarios. To overcome this challenge, a novel approach is proposed to enhance the viewing graph by resolving the relative orientations of images. By integrating this new method into a traditional continuous graph-based registration framework, a significant improvement in registration accuracy is achieved. Specifically, the approach is demonstrated to be effective in large-scale scenes, with results showing improved stability and accuracy. For example, the approach can accurately register images in a large, 3D city block with a high degree of precision. Additionally, the approach can also be applied to scenes with multiple, disconnected viewing graphs, where images can be successfully registered in a unified 3D space. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing baselines in both accuracy and robustness. The integration of unpredictable renewable energy sources into the power grid poses a challenge for power system operators, necessitating additional reserve resources to mitigate the risk of outages. To address this issue, this paper presents a dynamic reserve sizing model that incorporates real-time and probabilistic forecasts. The proposed approach is demonstrated using a modified 37-bus IEEE system, demonstrating its potential to reduce reserve requirements by up to 30% and decrease the likelihood of unnecessary reserve activation. The study also highlights the effectiveness of integrating advanced probabilistic forecasting techniques, such as ensemble methods and ARIMA models, to enhance the model's predictive capabilities. Ultimately, this model enables more efficient operation with increased reliability and reduced operational costs. To facilitate further research, this study provides open-source code for the model's training and simulation.
