In a scenario of $n$ competing individuals, each with a unique probability of winning, we're examining the length of time it takes for the winner to be declared, considering the case where contestants have equal chances of claiming the top spot. By deriving the probability distribution of this delayed outcome, we can apply it to model scenarios such as two-candidate elections, sports competitions with tied scores, and fantasy sports championships where scores are closely matched. Our analysis also reveals that, under certain conditions, the expected length of this wait period is a combination of both arithmetic and harmonic means. Specifically, if multiple contestants are tied for the minimum duration required to win, we've found that, on average, they'll take either the arithmetic or harmonic mean time to claim the top spot, with equal chances determined by the relative probabilities of winning and losing. Interestingly, this finding holds true even when there's no guarantee that the contestants will eventually win. To confirm our results, we've conducted extensive simulations and provided a real-world example of our theory in action. The insights gained from this research can be applied to a broader range of competitive events and provide valuable implications for decision-makers. Additionally, we've identified some potential avenues for further investigation and explored the connections between our work and other areas of probability theory. The code used in our simulations is freely available for public use. Overall, this study contributes to a deeper understanding of probability theory and its applications in analyzing complex competitive scenarios. This research presents Distributed Reward Learning (MSRL), a novel approach that integrates data stream analysis and reinforcement learning (RL) to develop a framework capable of processing continuous data streams. The system generates new data samples through data stream analysis, leveraging these to inform a reinforcement learning model. Initially, we outline the MSRL framework, highlighting its integration of data stream analysis and RL. We then discuss a key challenge associated with RL in a data stream, specifically the continuous nature of the stream. A novel temporal sampling (NTS) method is proposed to address this issue, where a temporal window of samples is selected from the stream. The NTS samples are used to develop a reward function, which is then utilized in a MSRL model. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of MSRL, contrasting it with existing methods and showing its superiority, before exploring its practical applications in reinforcement learning. The proposed framework is demonstrated in the context of a real-world problem, namely the development of a reinforcement learning model capable of predicting the direction of a stock price movement. The Gumbel-max algorithm is a widely used technique in variational inference (VI) that employs reparameterization to approximate the posterior distribution of uncertain discrete variables as samples. This method has seen extensive applications across various machine learning domains, particularly in natural language processing, computer vision, and reinforcement learning. Notably, the algorithm's efficiency has been enhanced through the development of novel extensions, such as the Gumbel-SBL method, which tackles sparse coding problems, and the Gumbel-softmax variant, which is commonly applied to one-hot encoded variables. This review paper delves into the Gumbel-SBL method, its underlying theory, and its real-world practicality. It also compares the Gumbel-softmax variant to its parent algorithm, which is also examined in detail, and its relevance in multiple machine learning contexts is explored. Ultimately, the survey concludes with a comprehensive analysis of the Gumbel-max method's current state and its potential directions for future research. We investigate the optimal transport problem with $\rho$-Wasserstein cost, which arises in scenarios involving congested transportation networks. Our results demonstrate that the dual problem of this transport cost can be solved using a specific type of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) known as the Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty. This particular GAN has a notable benefit in that it does not require the estimation of the gradient of the cost function, making it more robust and efficient. Our study focuses on the cost function $\rho$ and derives a bound on the gradient of the dual variable, which in turn leads to a convergence rate of $O(1/\sqrt{T})$ for the Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty. A novel approach to forecasting the variance of density fields in cosmology is presented through the Zel'dovich estimation technique. By leveraging the small-scale nature of this method to capture high-frequency cosmological information, it enables the creation of more accurate forecasts for cosmological parameters by minimizing the impact of large-scale cosmic web variances. Simulation-based tests confirm the efficacy of this method, particularly when applied to modestly sized simulations, and demonstrate that it yields results comparable to those obtained from larger-scale simulations, albeit at a significantly reduced computational cost. Furthermore, the Zel'dovich estimator's ability to detect subtle features, such as those present in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, is showcased, and it is shown that it can effectively identify these features, even when they are not fully captured by traditional power spectrum analyses. Ultimately, the Zel'dovich estimator emerges as a reliable tool for generating precise forecasts from limited simulation data. Future research directions involve exploring the potential of this method to be applied to real-world observations and actual galaxy catalogues. It's demonstrated that for such mixed graphs, the spectral radius is bounded by a function of the form $\sigma(M_1(M_3-1))$, where $M_1$ represents the spectral radius of a severed vertex in a mixed digon-free mixed graph with two distinct positive eigenvalues and $M_3$ is the spectral radius of the graph formed by combining severed vertices of the original mixed graph. Utilizing this bound, the class of mixed digon-free mixed graphs with severed vertices having two distinct positive eigenvalues is partially characterized. This paper introduces a novel approach to monocular 3D object recognition, leveraging a depth estimation module to dynamically generate informative object regions that adapt to varying distances. MPLS has been widely adopted for its efficient and scalable routing capabilities.  However, its widespread use also creates opportunities for malicious activities such as hiding malicious traffic, enabling anonymous DDoS attacks, and evading data protection regulations.  Recent research has shown that some MPLS attributes are visible from the outside, but this visibility is limited and does not provide a complete understanding of the system.  In contrast, our research proposes a novel approach called TNT, which uses passive measurement to identify MPLS tunnels and gather extensive data about them.  A custom-built tool using TNT was used to passively collect data on over 1,000 ASes, our findings indicate that TNT successfully uncovered the presence of 91% of the tunnels and obtained information on 78% of the subnets.  Furthermore, our analysis revealed that most tunnels are used for peering and content delivery networks, and that only a small fraction of the subnets (4.3%) are hidden.  In addition, our study found that the visibility of TNT was limited by issues such as misrouting, and the lack of visibility into some network layers.  This study highlights the need for a more effective approach to detect and identify MPLS tunnels, and underscores the importance of our proposed approach, TNT, in this regard.  Our study also shows that the current state of the art in this area is limited and that TNT offers a more effective solution. Neuromorphic photonic chips, specifically designed to mimic biological neurons, can potentially revolutionize the field of artificial intelligence by offering unparalleled processing capabilities. A key component of these devices is the optical matrix multiplier, which enables the parallel execution of complex matrix operations. However, the practical implementation of these chips remains a significant challenge, as researchers must develop practical frameworks to train and optimize photonic circuits. In this study, we compared the effectiveness of two training methods – local descent and evolutionary algorithms – to design and optimize optical matrix multipliers. Our results indicate that while local descent can quickly identify optimal circuit designs, it often leads to suboptimal solutions, whereas evolutionary algorithms yields more generalizable and robust solutions, albeit at a slower pace. Based on these findings, we recommend the use of evolutionary algorithms for designing optical matrix multipliers. Our study also highlights the limitations of current photonic devices and neural network models, which can serve as a starting point for further optimization and improvement. Ultimately, the development of more efficient neuromorphic photonic chips will require the integration of advanced machine learning techniques and innovative hardware designs. To address this issue, we have developed a novel algorithm called adaptive reinforced dynamics (ARD), which employs an adaptive time-rescaling technique to optimize simulations for energy exploration. By leveraging ARD, molecular dynamics simulations can be directed towards underpopulated regions of the energy surface, thereby accelerating convergence to the target temperature. The proposed method is versatile and can be integrated with any molecular dynamics simulation to generate more efficient sampling techniques for high-dimensional energy landscapes. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of ARD through its application to a challenging protein folding problem and a complex peptide binding scenario. When compared to alternative optimization techniques, our results show that ARD achieves substantial performance gains, resulting in accelerated convergence and improved energy exploration efficiency. When combined with thermodynamic integration, ARD simulations yield precise free energy differences with significantly reduced statistical errors. These findings indicate that ARD is a valuable tool for enhancing the efficiency of energy exploration simulations and can be widely utilized in biomolecular research. Advanced sensing technologies, such as computer vision and machine learning, are rapidly advancing to achieve human-level performance in perception and action. However, most existing datasets have limitations, primarily focusing on human-centric views from wearable devices or specific tasks in controlled environments. To address these issues, we introduce the Human-centric 4D Scene Dataset (HSC4D), which provides a comprehensive dataset of human-focusing views in various indoor and outdoor settings. By utilizing wearable inertial measurement units and LiDAR technology, we capture detailed 3D information of the environment and user activity. The HSC4D dataset features 1,000+ hours of data from 50 participants, including 30 hours of labeled human motion and 1,400 distinct activities. The dataset's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments using leading detection and tracking algorithms, as well as a 3D pose estimation model, which shows promising results. The HSC4D dataset is publicly available for research purposes at https://github.com/robot-perception-lab/HSC4D. The accompanying code and pre-processed data can be accessed at https://github.com/robot-perception-lab/hsc4d_data. The dataset's citation information can be found below. The objective of open-set identification is to determine when a sample originates from a known class or if it belongs to an unknown category. This problem is distinct from out-of-distribution detection, as it focuses on classifying samples into either in-distribution or out-of-distribution sets, without needing a separate, unknown dataset for training. Current approaches to OoD detection often involve training a model on a known set of in-distribution samples and an auxiliary set of unknown samples. However, these approaches have several limitations: they require a separate, unknown dataset, and they may not scale well as the size of the in-distribution set increases. This is because they rely on a two-class classifier, which can become less effective when the two classes have different densities. In contrast, our proposed method, Augment-driven Similarity Learning (ASL), uses a similarity metric to gauge the distance between known and unknown samples, and it does not require a separate, unknown dataset. This approach is more effective when the in-distribution and unknown samples are semantically similar, and it can be trained using a single dataset. Our experiments demonstrate that ASL outperforms existing methods in open-set identification tasks, particularly when the in-distribution and unknown samples are semantically similar. Additionally, our method achieves state-of-the-art results in OoD detection tasks, and it can be trained using a single dataset. Our code is available on GitHub. High-dimensional time series data is becoming increasingly prevalent in various scientific fields. Due to the complexity of handling vast amounts of data, effective dimensionality reduction techniques are essential for capturing key temporal characteristics. This paper introduces a novel method, FAVAR, which utilizes factor analysis to project high-dimensional time series data into a lower-dimensional space. The proposed FAVAR approach is distinct from existing factor modeling techniques in its ability to simultaneously model factor dynamics, leveraging high-dimensional data. We demonstrate the efficacy of FAVAR in capturing temporal data patterns through theoretical analysis and numerical results on simulated data. Furthermore, FAVAR has practical applications in analyzing high-dimensional temporal data from the Human Connectome Project. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach called Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator (ORCEC) and a developed dataset featuring various patterns of occlusions and light scattering.
